beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson nine. Connections to other pathways, and regulation. [[junction]]Picture a railway junction. Trains from many lines arrive, share a few tracks, and leave again on others. [[map]]Our respiration map works the same way. For eight lessons we followed one fuel, glucose, through it. [[inputs]]But a cell does not live on glucose alone. Today we light up the doors where other fuels come in, and then the dial that controls the whole map.
beats.inputs: [[carbs]]Carbohydrates are the easy case. Starch and other sugars are broken down to simple sugars, and glycolysis accepts a wide range of them. [[prot]]Proteins must first be digested to amino acids. Then the amino group is taken off, and it leaves as N H three. [[skel]]What remains is the carbon skeleton, and that is what feeds in. Some skeletons join at pyruvate, some become acetyl co-A, and some enter the citric acid cycle directly. The slide says the amino groups feed in, but it is the carbon skeletons that burn. The nitrogen leaves.
beats.fats: [[fat]]A fat is a glycerol head with three fatty acid tails. Digestion cuts them apart. [[gly]]Glycerol is a small three-carbon piece, and it enters glycolysis at glyceraldehyde three phosphate. [[fa]]The long fatty acid tails go through beta oxidation, which snips them two carbons at a time into acetyl co-A, ready for the citric acid cycle. [[twice]]Those tails are packed with energy. An oxidized gram of fat produces more than twice as much A T P as an oxidized gram of carbohydrate. [[gram]]A rough guide, not from the slides: about nine kilocalories per gram for fat, and about four for carbohydrate. That is why a body stores its long-term energy as fat. [[hubs]]So there are three kinds of food, but only a few doors: glycolysis, acetyl co-A, and the citric acid cycle. All of them lead on to oxidative phosphorylation.
beats.q1: Quick check. What does a fatty acid become on its way in?
beats.build: [[back]]The junction works in both directions. The body also has to build things: amino acids, fats, sugars, the parts of its own cells. This is biosynthesis, the anabolic pathways. [[small]]They draw their small molecules straight from food, or from glycolysis, or from the citric acid cycle. [[both]]So a molecule in the cycle can be burned for A T P, or pulled out and built into something new. Breaking down and building up share the same crossroads. That is why the cell must keep deciding which way the traffic goes.
beats.control: [[need]]Who decides? Not a manager, but feedback. [[dial]]If A T P begins to run low, respiration speeds up. If there is plenty of A T P, respiration slows down. The cell does this mainly by regulating the activity of enzymes at strategic points in the pathway. [[link]]You met the idea in chapter eight, lesson eight. Feedback inhibition is when an end product switches off its own pathway, as isoleucine switched off enzyme one. Here the end product is A T P, and the pathway is the whole respiration map. [[pfk]]The strategic point is an enzyme called phosphofructokinase, at the third step of glycolysis. It turns fructose six phosphate into fructose one, six bisphosphate, which commits the sugar to being split. It is the main valve of the map.
beats.valve: [[atp]]A T P inhibits it. When A T P is plentiful, it binds to phosphofructokinase and slows the valve, so less sugar is split. [[cit]]Citrate inhibits it too. Citrate is the first product of the citric acid cycle, so if citrate piles up, the cycle is full, and glycolysis can ease off. [[amp]]And A M P stimulates it. When A T P is used up, A M P builds up, a signal of low energy, and the valve opens wider. [[three]]Two brakes and one accelerator, all pressing on a single enzyme.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which molecule stimulates phosphofructokinase?
beats.loop: [[run]]Let's watch it work in a muscle fibre. [[spend]]The fibre contracts hard and spends A T P, so the A T P level falls and A M P rises. [[open]]A M P opens the valve. Glycolysis speeds up, more pyruvate flows into the mitochondrion, and oxidative phosphorylation makes A T P faster. [[rest]]Now the fibre rests. A T P is no longer used, so it builds up. [[close]]And that A T P loops back to phosphofructokinase and slows it. The map idles, and fuel is saved. Supply follows demand, and no one is in charge.
beats.wrap: To close the chapter, walk the map once more. [[r1]]In the cytosol, glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, with a small gain of A T P and N A D H. [[r2]]In the mitochondrion, pyruvate becomes acetyl co-A, and the citric acid cycle releases the carbon as carbon dioxide, loading up N A D H and F A D H two. [[r3]]Those carriers hand their electrons to the chain, which pumps protons, and A T P synthase turns their flow back into most of the cell's A T P. [[r4]]Without oxygen, fermentation keeps glycolysis going. [[r5]]And today: other fuels join at a few doors, and A T P itself closes the loop at phosphofructokinase. [[end]]Now try the practice.
